Fact.Name: Has itemized deductions
Fact.Description: Whether the taxpayer wants to report Schedule A itemized deductions. Gate for the Schedule A intake.

Fact.Name: Claims itemized deductions
Fact.Description: Complete-safe gate: true only when /hasItemizedDeductions is answered and true (IsComplete pattern, as qbi:/hasQualifiedTradeOrBusiness). California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).

Fact.Name: Election to itemize even though itemized deductions are less than the standard deduction (Schedule A line 18)
Fact.Description:
OPTIONAL §63(e) election — Schedule A line 18 ("If you elect to itemize deductions even though they are less than your standard deduction, check this box"). Answered TRUE with Schedule A claimed → itemized deductions are used on Form 1040 line 12 even when smaller than the standard deduction. Answered TRUE WITHOUT Schedule A claimed → the return is KNOCKED OUT (/knockoutElectToItemizeWithoutScheduleA) — an election the engine cannot honor must surface, never silently default (World #1). Unanswered or false: the larger of the itemized and standard deductions wins. NOTE on the MFS-spouse-itemizes case: that return is KNOCKED OUT upstream by the inherited /spouseItemizesKnockout regardless of this election — the election does NOT un-knock it (pairing the two is a follow-on decision). The election's reachable uses here: state-return optimization and any other voluntary §63(e) itemization.
[THE MFS NOTE ABOVE IS SUPERSEDED: the "follow-on decision" it defers has been made. filers:/spouseItemizesKnockout is DELETED, fact and all; IRC 63(c)(6)(A)'s zero is applied to standardDeduction:/standardDeduction by filers:/standardDeductionZeroedByMfsSpouseItemizing instead. For that filer the section 63(e) election is COMPULSORY rather than voluntary — with a zero standard deduction there is nothing to elect between, and 63(e)(1) still bars any itemized deduction without the election — which is why /itemizationIsCompulsoryUnderZeroStandardDeduction exists and why /knockoutElectToItemizeWithoutScheduleA now excludes them. The "reachable uses" sentence should therefore read: state-return optimization, any other voluntary section 63(e) itemization, AND the compulsory MFS case. ]

Fact.Name: Elects to itemize (complete-safe)
Fact.Description: /writableElectToItemize when answered, else false (the IsComplete pattern, as /claimsItemizedDeductions above).

Fact.Name: Knockout: elected to itemize but no Schedule A is claimed
Fact.Description: the §63(e) election was answered TRUE but the return claims no Schedule A itemized deductions — the engine has nothing to itemize, and silently ignoring an election is the World-#1 failure mode. BLOCKS SUBMISSION so the state surfaces.

Fact.Name: Itemizing is compulsory because this return's standard deduction is zero
Fact.Description:
True when filers:/standardDeductionZeroedByMfsSpouseItemizing is true — an MFS filer whose spouse itemizes, whose standard deduction IRC 63(c)(6)(A) sets to ZERO.
WHY THE SCHEDULE-A SIDE NEEDS A NAME OF ITS OWN. For this filer itemizing is not an ELECTION at all: with a zero standard deduction there is nothing to elect between, and 63(e)(1) still requires the election before any itemized deduction is allowed. So they answer /electsToItemize true and may have NOTHING to put on Schedule A, which makes /claimsItemizedDeductions false — the exact pair /knockoutElectToItemizeWithoutScheduleA fires on. That guard is narrowed by this fact rather than retired: the VOLUNTARY case, a filer with a positive standard deduction who elects to itemize and then says they do not want to report Schedule A deductions, is two answers that contradict each other, only the filer can say which is right, and the remedy is a corrected answer rather than a computation. That residue is a correct refusal and it stays.
NEITHER HALF LANDS ALONE: filling filers:/standardDeductionZeroedByMfsSpouseItemizing while this guard stood would make a return fileable and then refuse it one line later.
THE OPEN QUESTION THIS FILL DOES NOT PRETEND TO SETTLE: whether the freed filer's Schedule A total of $0 should be REPORTED as a Schedule A at all, or whether the return carries the zero without the schedule. Nothing printed settles it; the dictionary computes the zero either way, and which forms are rendered is not this fact's decision.

Fact.Name: Medical and dental expenses
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 1: unreimbursed medical and dental expenses.
Do not include any amount you deducted as a self-employed health insurance premium on Form 7206 line 14 (Schedule 1 line 17) — IRC section 162(l)(3) forbids taking the same premiums into account here. This dictionary does not currently compute or check that overlap; if you paid premiums under a Form 7206 plan AND itemize, do not enter those premiums in this box.
If any amount you entered here was also deducted on Form 7206 line 14, enter that duplicated amount in the separate coordination question. If you already excluded all of those premiums from the total above, answer $0 to that question.

Fact.Name: Schedule A medical expenses also deducted on Form 7206 line 14
Fact.Description: Amount of the Schedule A medical and dental expenses entered above that was also deducted on Form 7206 line 14.

Fact.Name: Schedule A medical expenses after Form 7206 coordination
Fact.Description: Schedule A medical expenses after subtracting the amount also deducted on Form 7206 line 14. The overlap answer is an OPTIONAL intake: when it is unanswered on a return that has both a positive Schedule A medical total and a positive Form 7206 line 14, this fact carries the entered medical total unchanged, exactly as it did before the coordination existed, and /knockoutForm7206MedicalExpenseOverlap — a member of flow:/flowIsKnockedOut — blocks submission instead. A new intake must not leave itemized deductions, taxable income and the credit chain Incomplete on a return that pre-dates it. An ANSWERED overlap that contradicts its own sources — larger than the Schedule A total or larger than Form 7206 line 14 — still leaves this fact Incomplete: that is the return's own input, and house rule 5 is exactly about those. The overlap amount is declared non-negative; floor the subtrahend at $0 so an invalid negative seed cannot inflate the coordinated expense total.

Fact.Name: Schedule A medical expenses paid with tax-free HSA or MSA distributions
Fact.Description: Question: "How much of the medical and dental expenses you entered for Schedule A line 1 did you pay (or were you reimbursed for) with distributions from a health savings account (HSA), an Archer MSA or a Medicare Advantage MSA?" Help text: expenses paid with an HSA or MSA distribution for qualified medical expenses are not deductible medical expenses on Schedule A, so they are removed from the line 1 total. If you already left them out of the amount you entered, answer $0. Asked when the return itemizes, enters Schedule A medical expenses above $0, and reports an HSA distribution (Form 1099-SA) or an Archer or Medicare Advantage MSA distribution (Form 8853 line 7 or line 11) that paid qualified medical expenses. Unanswered on such a return: Schedule A line 1 and everything that reads it stay unresolved until it is answered (no default). Validation: dollars, not less than $0, not more than the medical total entered.

Fact.Name: Schedule A medical expenses after removing HSA- and MSA-paid amounts
Fact.Description:
/medicalExpensesAfterForm7206Coordination less the amount the filer says an HSA, Archer MSA or Medicare Advantage MSA distribution paid (/writableMedicalExpensesPaidWithHsaOrMsaDistributions, floored at $0): an expense paid out of an HSA or an Archer MSA (a Medicare Advantage MSA is one) for qualified medical expenses is not an expense paid for medical care for the Schedule A deduction. The removal comes before the Publication 570 territory apportionment in /allowableMedicalExpenses and before the 7.5 percent AGI floor.
Unchanged from /medicalExpensesAfterForm7206Coordination on every return that reports no HSA or MSA distribution paying qualified medical expenses (hsa /hsaDistributionsPaidQualifiedMedicalExpenses and /msaDistributionsPaidQualifiedMedicalExpenses both false), that does not itemize, or whose medical total is $0. On an itemizing return with a positive medical total and an HSA or MSA distribution that paid qualified medical expenses, the HSA- or MSA-paid amount is a required answer: unanswered, or answered above the medical total, this fact is Incomplete and the return is held rather than filed with the same expense counted twice.

Fact.Name: Form 7206 and Schedule A medical-expense overlap is unresolved
Fact.Description: Submission guard for an itemized return whose ANSWERED Form 7206 / Schedule A medical overlap contradicts its own sources — larger than the Schedule A medical total, or larger than Form 7206 line 14. RULING 6 WITHDREW THE UNANSWERED ARM: a refusal guard may never fire on an unanswered intake, and the application does not ask this question yet, so the withdrawn arm refused every itemizing return that had both a medical total and a positive line 14. An unanswered overlap leaves /medicalExpensesAfterForm7206Coordination at the entered medical total, which is the behaviour of a return that pre-dates the intake.

Fact.Name: State and local taxes paid
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 5d: state and local income-or-sales, real estate, and personal property taxes combined. Leave out foreign real property taxes and foreign personal property taxes: section 164(b)(6)(A) bars foreign real property taxes for 2018 through 2025, and the instructions list foreign personal or real property taxes among the taxes you can't deduct (a foreign income tax goes on line 6 or to the foreign tax credit). Other taxes (line 6) reach line 7 through the /writableScheduleALine6OtherTaxes intake and /scheduleALine7TotalTaxes.
NOT THE DIRECT SOURCE OF LINE 5d, BUT ITS FALLBACK. The 5a/5b/5c split IS modelled (the sentence saying it is not is superseded). /scheduleALine5dStateAndLocalTaxes is the printed line: it adds the three components when the filer answered 5a or 5c, and reads THIS fact otherwise. Nothing consumes this fact directly any more except that fall through arm, so a filer who answers both paths is not deducted twice. The sales tax election itself is still unmodelled and is recorded at /writableScheduleALine5aElectsGeneralSalesTaxes.
LEAVE OUT the real estate taxes you entered on Form 8829 for a home you use for a business (scheduleC:/scheduleCs/*/writableForm8829IndirectRealEstateTaxes): the return adds their personal part (scheduleC:/form8829PersonalHomeRealEstateTaxesTotal) and puts the business part on Form 8829.

Fact.Name: Home mortgage interest and points
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 8e: home mortgage interest and points. The $750,000 acquisition-debt limit is attested by the filer, not modeled. Investment interest (line 9) is not modelled.
NOT THE DIRECT SOURCE OF LINE 8e, BUT ITS FALLBACK. The Form 1098 reporting detail IS collected, on lines 8a, 8b and 8c (the sentence saying it is not modelled is superseded). /scheduleALine8eHomeMortgageInterestAndPoints is the printed line: it adds the three components when the filer answered any of them, and reads THIS fact otherwise. Nothing consumes this fact directly any more except that fall through arm, so a filer who answers both paths is not deducted twice.
LEAVE OUT the mortgage interest you entered on Form 8829 for a home you use for a business (within scheduleC:/scheduleCs/*/writableForm8829IndirectMortgageInterestAndTaxes): the return adds its personal part (scheduleC:/form8829PersonalHomeMortgageInterestTotal) and puts the business part on Form 8829.

Fact.Name: Gross income from all sources, complete-safe Schedule A value
Fact.Description: Passes the income denominator through only when the income intake is answered; an unanswered denominator is the complete-safe zero used by Schedule A's optional possession-exclusion apportionment. The source remains the income module's writable and this local alias only prevents an incomplete selector from falling through to a raw value.

Fact.Name: Medical and dental expenses allowable on Schedule A line 1 after the Pub. 570 apportionment
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 1 as ENTERED: /writableMedicalExpenses apportioned by the Publication 570 chapter 4 fraction when the return excludes section 931/933 territory income, and the raw entry otherwise.
WHY THE APPORTIONMENT LANDS ON THE INPUT AND NOT ON THE LINE-4 SUBTOTAL, which is the load-bearing placement choice: the publication says "Enter on Schedule A (Form 1040) only the allowable portion of each deduction" and its worked example enters the apportioned figures ON lines 1, 5b, 8a and 11 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 34). Schedule A's own limits then run on top. THAT ORDER IS NOT STYLISTIC: the medical deduction is gross expenses less 7.5 percent of AGI, a NONLINEAR floor, so apportioning before the floor and apportioning after it give different answers, and only the first is what the publication prescribes.
THE WITNESS IS THE PUBLICATION'S OWN PRINTED OUTPUT: 96,000/120,000 times 11,000 = 8,800, "enter on line 1 of Schedule A" (lines 2344-2348).
Complete-safe by construction: with no exclusion, or with the gross-income denominator unanswered, this IS /writableMedicalExpenses, so no committed return moves.
For an itemized return with a positive Form 7206 line 14 amount and positive medical expenses, the line 1 amount is /medicalExpensesAfterForm7206Coordination before the same territory apportionment; that removal remains before Schedule A's 7.5% AGI floor. The figure read here is /medicalExpensesAfterHsaCoordination, which also removes the amount an HSA or MSA distribution paid (IRC 223(f)(6), 220(f)(6)) and equals the Form 7206-coordinated total on every return without one. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).

Fact.Name: Home mortgage interest allowable on Schedule A after the Pub. 570 apportionment
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 8a/8e as ENTERED: /scheduleALine8eHomeMortgageInterestAndPoints apportioned by the Publication 570 chapter 4 fraction when the return excludes section 931/933 territory income, and the raw entry otherwise. Same placement argument as /allowableMedicalExpenses above.
THE LINE 8e TERM IS NOT THE RAW COMBINED INTAKE: it is /scheduleALine8eHomeMortgageInterestAndPoints, which adds the printed components 8a, 8b and 8c when the filer split them out and falls through to /writableMortgageInterest otherwise. A return that never answers one of the three reads the same number it read before.
IT FEEDS /mortgageInterestDeductionAfterCredit, WHICH THEN SUBTRACTS THE FORM 8396 CREDIT, and the order is APPORTION-THEN-SUBTRACT deliberately: that reduction is a double-benefit rule about the credit the filer actually claims, which is a fixed dollar amount rather than a share of income. Apportioning the NET would shrink that fixed subtraction by the same fraction and under-remove the double benefit.
THE WITNESS IS THE PUBLICATION'S OWN PRINTED OUTPUT: 96,000/120,000 times 16,250 = 13,000, "enter on line 8a of Schedule A" (lines 2354-2357).
Complete-safe by construction, exactly as above.
THE APPORTIONED TERM IS NOW THE TRACED ONE. /scheduleALine8eHomeMortgageInterestAndPoints is no longer read here directly; the term is /scheduleAMortgageQualifyingInterestAndPoints, the same entered total LESS the validated non-acquisition portion the filer attests on the new /writableScheduleALine8NonqualifyingInterestAndPoints. Pub 936 Table 1 line 13 asks for "the total amount of interest that you paid on the loans from line 12" -- the loans on lines 1, 2 and 7 -- so tracing has to come off BEFORE both the apportionment and the debt ratio. On a return that answers neither the tracing exclusion nor the mixed-use checkbox, the exclusion is a complete-safe $0 and this fact reads exactly what it read before. The witness above (13,000) is unchanged and still passes. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540) Part II line 8 California mortgage-interest limits).

Fact.Name: Average balance of home acquisition debt incurred after December 15, 2017
Fact.Description:
Pub 936 Table 1 line 7: the average balance during the year of the home mortgage debt used to buy, build, or substantially improve a qualified home, for debt taken out after December 15, 2017 (the population the $750,000/$375,000-MFS acquisition debt limit applies to). Table 1's Average Mortgage Balance worksheet computes this figure from monthly statements; this module asks for the RESULT rather than re-deriving it from monthly balances, the same attestation posture the module already uses for the mortgage loan proceeds question. SCOPE: this module tracks only the post-December-15-2017 tranche (Table 1 line 7) -- grandfathered debt (line 1) and pre-December-16-2017 acquisition debt (line 2) are NOT separately asked, so a filer whose ONLY debt predates December 16, 2017 answers $0 here and is treated as unlimited by this fact, the correct outcome for that population (their debt is capped at the higher $1,000,000/$500,000-MFS grandfathered limit, which this module does not separately test but which the overwhelming majority of such balances do not exceed). A filer who combines large grandfathered debt with large post-2017 debt near or over the modern cap is a residual this fact does not capture; disclosed, not modeled. Asked only when the filer claims mortgage interest greater than $0 (/scheduleALine8eHomeMortgageInterestAndPoints) -- a return that claims none never sees this question. A CLAIMING return that leaves this unanswered refuses the deduction Incomplete rather than assuming the debt is under the cap. Dollar, non-negative.
THE SCOPE PARAGRAPH ABOVE IS SUPERSEDED IN PART. Table 1 lines 1 (grandfathered) and 2 (pre-December-16-2017 acquisition debt) are now separately asked, on /writableScheduleALine8AverageGrandfatheredDebtBalance and /writableScheduleALine8AveragePre2018AcquisitionDebtBalance. Answering EITHER of them selects the detailed Table 1 path, in which this balance is Table 1 line 7 and all three categories plus the filing status must be answered. Answering NEITHER leaves the legacy post-2017-only computation exactly as described above, zero-balance bypass included -- which is why the residual population named above (large grandfathered debt combined with large post-2017 debt) is now buildable rather than merely disclosed. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540) Part II line 8 California $1,000,000 debt fraction).

Fact.Name: Home acquisition debt qualified loan limit (Pub 936 Table 1 line 8)
Fact.Description: Pub 936 Table 1 line 8: $750,000, or $375,000 if the filer's status is married filing separately. Simplified to Table 1 line 8 directly (rather than working lines 1-11 in full) because this module does not separately track grandfathered or pre-December-16- 2017 acquisition debt (see /writableScheduleALine8AverageAcquisitionDebtBalance) -- with lines 1 and 2 at $0, line 6 is $0, so line 9 (the larger of line 6 or line 8) is always line 8 itself, and line 11 (the smaller of line 9 or line 10 = line 6 + line 7) reduces to the smaller of line 8 and the post-2017 average balance alone. Filing status is asked at the start of every real return, so this defaults to the non-MFS $750,000 limit only in the degenerate case of a return with no filing status at all -- not a genuine condition of allowance the way the debt balance itself is.

Fact.Name: Home mortgage interest allowable after the section 163(h)(3) acquisition debt limit
Fact.Description:
/allowableMortgageInterest (the Pub 570-apportioned line 8e figure) reduced, when it exceeds the qualified loan limit, by the Pub 936 Table 1 Part II ratio: qualified loan limit divided by the average balance of the debt the limit applies to (Table 1 lines 11 and 12; this module's line 12 is the same average balance as line 7, since it does not separately track grandfathered or pre-2017 debt, so lines 11/12 reduce to min(limit, balance) / balance). Deductible interest = interest paid x that ratio, rounded.
NOT CLAIMING is complete-safe: a return that never claims mortgage interest, or claims exactly $0, passes /allowableMortgageInterest through unchanged and never asks the average balance question.
CLAIMING (mortgage interest greater than $0) makes the average acquisition debt balance a genuine condition of allowance: answered and at or under the qualified loan limit (or answered $0, meaning no post-2017 acquisition debt is attested) passes the interest through UNCAPPED; answered over the limit applies the Table 1 ratio; UNANSWERED refuses this fact Incomplete rather than silently assuming the debt is under the cap.
THE RATIO IS A NAMED FACT, /scheduleAMortgageDebtLimitFractionPerThousand, WITH TWO ARMS. It carries Table 1 line 14 (limit / average debt, three decimal places, stored x1000). Its LEGACY arm — min(limit, balance)/balance with the answered-zero bypass — is chosen when neither older-debt balance is answered. Its DETAILED arm is Table 1 line 11 / line 12 over all three categories. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540) Part II line 8 California mortgage-interest limits).

Fact.Name: Home mortgage interest deduction after the Form 8396 mortgage interest credit reduction (Schedule A line 8e)
Fact.Description: Schedule A line 8e home mortgage interest (/writableMortgageInterest) REDUCED by the current-year Form 8396 mortgage interest credit (Form 8396 line 3, /form8396TentativeCredit), floored at 0. DOUBLE BENEFIT: Form 8396 states "you must reduce your deduction for home mortgage interest on Schedule A by the amount on line 3" — the interest that generates the MCC credit is the SAME interest deducted on line 8e, so deducting it in full while also crediting it is a prohibited double benefit. Reduces /allowableMortgageInterestAfterDebtLimit (the section 163(h)(3) acquisition-debt-limited figure), not the raw entered amount, so the credit reduction and the debt limit compose correctly regardless of order. The reduction is by LINE 3 (the current-year tentative credit), NOT the tax-liability-limited allowed credit (Form 8396 line 9): the form says to reduce "even if part of the amount on line 3 is carried forward to 2026", and — decisive for acyclicity — line 3 depends only on the MCC writables (interest × rate, capped), never on tax or on the Schedule A total, so no cycle is introduced (the allowed credit, which runs through the tax-liability Credit Limit Worksheet, WOULD cycle). /form8396TentativeCredit is complete-safe 0 without an MCC, so every non-MCC return keeps this = /writableMortgageInterest byte-identical; and GreaterOf(Subtract(w, c), 0) propagates /writableMortgageInterest's incompleteness (ReduceOperator/BinaryOperator short-circuit on Incomplete), so the itemized-total completeness is unchanged. interpretation:provisional. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).

Fact.Name: Gifts to charity by cash or check (to public charities)
Fact.Description: Schedule A line 11: cash/check gifts to 50%-limit (public) charities. US8-4 now MODELS the 60%-of-AGI limit on this amount (was attested). SCOPE: cash to 30%-limit organizations (private nonoperating foundations) is NOT separately modeled — enter only public-charity cash here. SCOPE CARVE: this is the gift the FILER made. It EXCLUDES a partnership's or S corporation's pass-through share reported in Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) box 13 code A or Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) box 12 code A, which /k1CharitableCash60Pct now totals from the recorded documents and adds to this tier beside this entry through /charitableCashIncludingK1. Entering that amount here as well would state the same gift twice. The graph cannot tell a double entry from a genuinely larger direct gift, which is why the carve is stated on the intake rather than enforced in arithmetic.

Fact.Name: Gifts to charity other than cash (capital gain property to public charities)
Fact.Description: Schedule A line 12: capital-gain property (held > 1 year) given at FMV to 50%-limit (public) charities. US8-4 now MODELS the 30%-of-AGI limit on this amount (was attested). NOT HERE: ordinary income property and capital gain property whose value you reduced under the capital gain property election (both go on /writableCharitable50PctOrgNonCash, Worksheet 2 line 9, under the 50%-of-AGI limit), gifts to 30%-limit organizations, and qualified conservation contributions. If you make the capital gain property election, it applies to all capital gain property you gave to 50%-limit organizations this year, so none of it is entered here. The prior-year carryover-IN (line 13) IS now applied as an attested writable (/charitableCarryoverInDeductible), but the carry-OUT re-computation of an unused carryover-IN is not modelled; this year's own excess is REPORTED as /charitableCarryover. SCOPE CARVE: this is the gift the FILER made. It EXCLUDES a partnership's or S corporation's pass-through share reported in Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) box 13 code E or Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) box 12 code E, which /k1CharitableCapGain50PctOrg totals from the recorded documents and adds to this tier beside this entry through /charitableNonCashIncludingK1. Entering that amount here as well would state the same gift twice. Code C (noncash contributions, 50%) is not part of this tier: it joins Worksheet 2 line 9 through /charitable50PctOrgNonCashIncludingK1.

Fact.Name: Noncash gifts to 50% limit organizations other than capital gain property deducted at FMV
Fact.Description: Publication 526 Worksheet 2 line 9 for tax year 2025: noncash gifts to 50% limit (public) charities that are NOT capital gain property deducted at its fair market value. It covers ordinary income property (for example used clothing and household goods, inventory, or property held one year or less), and capital gain property to a 50% limit organization whose fair market value you reduced by its appreciation under the capital gain property election. Enter the amount AFTER the required reduction: for ordinary income property, its fair market value minus the gain that would not have been long-term capital gain had you sold it (usually your basis); for elected capital gain property, its fair market value minus the appreciation (its basis). These gifts are deductible up to 50% of adjusted gross income minus the cash gifts to 50% limit organizations you deduct, and any excess carries over. Do not enter here capital gain property you deduct at fair market value (that is the capital gain property entry), gifts to organizations that are not 50% limit organizations, gifts "for the use of" an organization, qualified conservation contributions, or an amount a partnership or S corporation reported to you on Schedule K-1 (box 13 or box 12 code C), which the return takes from the recorded K-1. If you make the capital gain property election, it applies to all capital gain property you gave to 50% limit organizations this year. Dollar, not negative. Optional: a return with no such gift leaves it unanswered.

Fact.Name: Noncash gifts to 50% limit organizations other than capital gain property at FMV, complete-safe view
Fact.Description: /writableCharitable50PctOrgNonCash when the filer answered it, else $0, so a return that never answers the question keeps every charitable line exactly as complete as before.

Fact.Name: Charitable contribution carryover from prior year (Schedule A line 13)
Fact.Description: Schedule A line 13: the prior-year charitable contribution carryover the filer attests (the part of an earlier year's gifts the AGI limits disallowed, still within its 5-year window — Pub 526 "Carryovers"). This input models it as a SINGLE attested carryover-IN amount: the cash-vs-capital-gain CHARACTER the carryover keeps in reality (Pub 526: a carryover keeps the percentage limit of its origin year) is NOT separately modeled — a single blended amount deducted within the 50%-of-AGI overall ceiling is an accepted simplification (surfaced, provisional). Optional — a return with no prior-year carryover never answers this (complete-safe downstream).

Fact.Name: Prior-year CASH charitable carryover (Schedule A line 13, 60%-tier character)
Fact.Description: The CASH-character part of a prior-year charitable carryover — a gift of cash to a 50%-limit (public-charity) organization that an earlier year's 60%-of-AGI limit disallowed, still within its 5-year window. A carryover keeps the percentage limit of its origin category (Pub 526 "Carryovers": "subject to the same percentage limits in the year to which they are carried"), so a cash carryover is deducted this year within the 60%-of-AGI CASH ceiling — NOT the 50% overall ceiling the blended /writableCharitableCarryoverFromPriorTaxYear conservatively uses. Use THIS input (and its capital-gain twin) when the carryover's character is known; the blended input stays as the unknown-character conservative fallback (do not set both). Optional — complete-safe downstream (a return with no cash carryover never answers this).

Fact.Name: Prior-year CAPITAL-GAIN-property charitable carryover (Schedule A line 13, 30%-tier)
Fact.Description: The CAPITAL-GAIN-property part of a prior-year charitable carryover — a gift of appreciated capital-gain property to a 50%-limit organization that an earlier year's 30%-of-AGI limit disallowed. Deducted this year within the 30%-of-AGI capital-gain ceiling (its origin-category limit, Pub 526 "Carryovers"), and never beyond the overall 50%-of-AGI ceiling after the higher tiers. Use with its cash twin when character is known; the blended input is the unknown-character fallback (do not set both). Optional — complete-safe downstream. No published Pub 526 numeric example for the capital-gain carryover tier (ai-only), so the goldens are placed where the 30% own-limit binds.

Fact.Name: Prior-year CASH charitable carryover contributed in 2020 (Schedule A line 13, dated lot)
Fact.Description:
THE DATED CARRY-IN, CASH character, 2020 vintage. The part of the filer's prior-year charitable carryover that originates in 2020 gifts of cash to 50%-limit (public-charity) organizations, deducted this year within the 60%-of-AGI cash ceiling its origin category carries. Five such slots per character (2020-2024) are exactly TY2025's surviving vintages, and they are consumed OLDEST-FIRST: "If you have carryovers from 2 or more prior years, use the carryover from the earlier year first." 2020 IS THE OLDEST SURVIVING VINTAGE: 2025 is its fifth and last succeeding year, so anything this lot does not use this year EXPIRES (reported by /charitableCarryoverExpiredUnused). There is deliberately no 2019 slot - the closed slot set IS the 5-year window, enforced at the intake boundary rather than by a derivation.
WHY THE PATH NAMES THE YEAR. The filer reads a contribution year off a document they already hold, so a year-named slot is a direct transcription with no arithmetic to get wrong, and it is the idiom the IRS itself prints (Form 8396 lines 4-6, "Enter any 2022 credit carryforward ... 2023 ... 2024", consumed "beginning with the earliest prior year", renamed annually by the IRS). REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: age-named slots (age1..age5), which would roll to TY2026 with zero renames. They were rejected because a slot's MEANING would then move under a persisted answer - "age 5" is 2020 this year and 2021 next year - so a stored fact graph carried forward would silently RE-DATE money, whereas a year-named path simply ceases to exist and fails loudly; and because the 2021 exception is anchored to a CALENDAR year, so an age-named graph would need an annual edit to move it regardless.
MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with the undated carry-IN writables. Answering ANY vintage slot moves the whole Schedule A line 13 intake onto the dated path and suppresses all three undated writables to $0 in the graph, extending the mutual-exclusion idiom one level. Optional - a return with no dated carryover never answers this (complete-safe downstream).
NOT A SLOT FOR A QUALIFIED CONSERVATION CONTRIBUTION, stated here rather than left silent. A QCC carryover runs FIFTEEN years, not five - Pub. 526, "A carryover of a qualified conservation contribution can be carried forward for 15 years" - so the five-slot window this fact belongs to is wrong for one, and a QCC lot contributed before 2020 has no slot at all. QCC is already a stated scope-out of the CURRENT-YEAR intake (/writableCharitableNonCash), so nothing in this module models one in either direction. Fact.Name: Cash charitable contributions allowable after the Pub. 570 apportionment
Fact.Description:
Schedule A charitable contributions as ENTERED: /writableCharitableCash apportioned by the Publication 570 chapter 4 fraction when the return excludes section 931/933 territory income, and the raw entry otherwise. APPORTIONED AT THE CONTRIBUTION, BEFORE EVERY AGI LIMIT, and that ordering is the whole correctness question for this tier machinery. Publication 570's worked example enters the apportioned figure ON Schedule A line 11 and says "Enter on Schedule A (Form 1040) only the allowable portion of each deduction" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 34); the 60/30/20-percent-of-AGI limits and the cross-caps then run on top. The two orders are NOT equal whenever a limit binds: apportioning first gives min(0.8C, 0.6*AGI), apportioning the finished deduction would give 0.8*min(C, 0.6*AGI), and AGI itself does not move because the excluded income was never in it. Only the first is what the publication prescribes.
EVERY CONSUMER OF THE RAW WRITABLE WAS RE-POINTED, not a subset — a partial re-point would feed one worksheet a mix of apportioned and raw amounts, which is a defect no single test would localise. The re-point is scripted with an asserted occurrence count so a structural change to this module breaks loudly instead of silently leaving a site behind.
⚠ CARRYOVERS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT APPORTIONED, and this is the one place this fill guesses least by refusing to guess. The eleven /writableCharitable*CarryoverFromPriorTaxYear intakes are untouched. Publication 570 says nothing about a carryover, and there are two defensible readings — apportion by THIS year's fraction because the deduction arises this year, or leave it because the contribution was already tested in its own year. Choosing silently would bury a judgement inside arithmetic. Direction if the first reading is right: the carryover is UNDER-apportioned and the deduction too large, taxpayer-favourable.
Complete-safe by construction: with no exclusion, or with the gross-income denominator unanswered, this IS the raw writable, so no committed return moves.

Fact.Name: Attested prior-year carryover of contributions to 50%-limit organizations
Fact.Description:
The Schedule A line 13 carryover-IN the filer attested, as a single amount, for use in the OVERALL-CEILING SUBTRAHEND of the two 30%-limit-organization tiers. Pub 526 states an ordering rule that the tiers were missing: "A carryover of a contribution to a 50% limit organization must be used before contributions in the current year to organizations other than 50% limit organizations." So when the 30%-org tiers ask how much of the 50%-of-AGI ceiling is already spoken for, the answer includes the carryover, not only the current-year 50%-org gifts.
WHY THE TIERS DID NOT HAVE THIS, and it is not that the earlier author misread a rule. Both 30%-org tiers implement Pub 526 Worksheet 2 (step 3b at worksheet line 20, step 5d at worksheet line 33) faithfully, and Worksheet 2 has NO CARRYOVER ROW anywhere in its 52 lines. It could not have one: the worksheet opens with "Caution: Don't use this worksheet to figure the contributions you can deduct this year if you have a carryover of a charitable contribution from an earlier year." The worksheet is simply not the instrument for a carryover return, and the narrative Note plus Carryovers Example 2 is. That is why the terms this fact feeds MUST be zero when no carryover is answered — the guard is not defensive, it is what keeps the faithful Worksheet 2 reading intact on every no-carryover return, which is every committed scenario that reaches those tiers.
THE ATTESTED AMOUNT, NOT THE DEDUCTIBLE, AND THAT CHOICE IS FORCED. Pub 526 Example 2 cannot settle it — there the carryover is deductible in full, so the two coincide at $5,000. Two other things settle it. (1) ACYCLICITY: the carryover deductibles already subtract both 30%-org deductibles (see /charitableCapGainCarryoverInDeductible's overall term), so a tier that subtracted a carryover DEDUCTIBLE would close a cycle. Only the writables, which depend on nothing, break it. (2) CONSISTENCY: the tiers' existing subtrahend already uses the full 50%-org WRITABLES rather than their AGI-limited deductibles, which is what Worksheet 2 step 3b specifies, and Example 2's own $11,000 is likewise a sum of CONTRIBUTIONS ("the sum of your current and carryover contributions to 50% limit organizations, $6,000 + $5,000"). Rejected alternative: the three carryover deductibles, which matches Example 2 equally well on its own numbers and cycles. DIRECTION where the two diverge (a carryover not deductible in full): using the larger attested amount over-subtracts, so the 30%-org tier is held DOWN and the excess flows to /charitableCarryover rather than being deducted — taxpayer-adverse this year, never an over-deduction, and the amount is preserved as a carry-out rather than lost.
MUTUAL EXCLUSION MIRRORED, not re-derived: Schedule A line 13 is modeled three ways and they are made exclusive in the graph, with the blended /writableCharitableCarryoverFromPriorTaxYear suppressed to $0 whenever either character-split writable is answered. This fact's blended leg goes to $0 on exactly that condition, so a filer who answered both cannot have the same carryover pool counted twice in the subtrahend. Each leg is separately IsComplete-guarded, as in /charitableCarryoverToNextYear, because a filer may answer one character and not the other and an unguarded read would send this fact — and through it both 30%-org tiers — Incomplete by contagion.
COMPLETE-SAFE AND $0 on every return with no carryover, which is every committed scenario that answers a 30%-org writable (the 30%-org and carry-IN fixture sets are disjoint), so the two tiers it feeds are byte-identical on the committed corpus. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).

TERMS (c) AND (d) ARE A CORRECTION, NOT AN EXTENSION: without them the tier is not conservative. Worksheet lines 36 and 37 are printed rows of the line-40 smallest-of; a term inside a smallest-of can only REDUCE the result, so omitting two of them is not conservative — it OVER-deducts, silently, with no refusal anywhere in the graph.
WORKSHEET-LITERAL SUBTRAHENDS. Terms (c) and (d) subtract the DEDUCTIBLE amounts (worksheet lines 30 and 24), because worksheet lines 37 and 36 name those "Deductible amount" rows by number. The narrative at "Limit Based on 20% of AGI" instead says "minus your contributions", which would be MORE adverse; that is the rejected alternative, and the worksheet wins because Pub 526 says of its own narrative steps "These steps are incorporated into Worksheet 2." The caps move the current-year tiers and never the carry-IN.
STILL NO PUBLISHED NUMERIC EXAMPLE for this tier: Pub 526 prints none for the 20% limit, so the tag stays ai-only even though every term is now a verbatim printed worksheet row. What changed is that the tier no longer carries a DEPARTURE from the printed rows — only a missing witness for them.

Fact.Name: The attested 50%-org carryover read off the vintage slots (all ten, complete-safe)
Fact.Description:
The dated-path replacement for the three undated writables inside /attestedCharitableCarryoverIn50PctOrgs. Pub. 526's Carryovers Note puts a carryover to a 50%-limit organization AHEAD of current-year gifts to organizations that are NOT 50%-limit organizations, so the two 30%-limit-organization tiers must subtract the carryover from their overall-ceiling headroom. Both carryover characters this module models are gifts to 50%-limit organizations (cash to a public charity; capital-gain property to a 50%-limit organization), so all ten slots belong in the sum, exactly as all three undated writables do today.

On the dated path a filer typically answers ONE slot; an unguarded read of the other nine would send this fact Incomplete, and through it both 30%-org tiers and Schedule A line 14 — on every return in the corpus. Complete-safe $0 when no slot is answered, which is every committed case.

Fact.Description:

The boundary is age-5-allows / age-6-denies: there is no 2019 slot to answer at all.
THIS IS THE NUMBER THE UNDATED CARRY-OUT COULD NEVER REPORT, and it is the whole point of dating the lots. The shipping /charitableCarryoverToNextYear tells a filer what survived the CEILINGS; only a dated model can tell them what did not survive the CALENDAR. Reported, never deducted, and deliberately absent from /charitableCarryoverSlotsToNextYear — carrying it would be exactly the over-statement the undated model was disclosed as risking.
Exported and consumed by nothing this year. Complete-safe $0 when neither 2020 slot is answered, which is every committed case.

Fact.Description:

WHAT THIS FACT DOES NOT DO, stated plainly because the dated model makes it easy to over-read. It does not re-index the vintages for next year (a 2021 lot is /charitableCarryoverResidue2021 here and would be a 2021 slot in a TY2026 dictionary, which is a per-year dictionary by construction), and it does not tell next year's return anything about the SEVEN situations Pub. 526 lists and then declines to discuss — see the authority note below, which is an authority gap SURFACED, not modelled. SEVEN, not six, counted off the vendored page. The seventh is "become a surviving spouse", which is a fifth marital-change case rather than a duplicate of the other four.
Complete-safe $0 when no slot is answered. Reported through /charitableCarryoverToNextYear on the dated path.

Fact.Name: Qualified conservation contribution (QCC)
Fact.Description:
A contribution of a qualified real property interest -- a restriction on the use of real property, granted in perpetuity -- to a qualified organization exclusively for conservation purposes. Coordinated OUTSIDE every other charitable tier (IRC 170(b)(1)(E)(iii)): a QCC's own ceiling is 50% of AGI (100% for a qualifying farmer or rancher, see /writableCharitableQualifiedFarmerOrRancher) minus the filer's OTHER current-year charitable deductions, tested separately from the 60/50/30/20-percent tiers rather than folded into any of them. Asked as its own box, not a slot on the ordinary noncash-property gift questions, because the ceiling formula and the farmer/rancher branch are unique to this population. Optional -- a return with no such gift never answers this and stays byte-identical to a return with no QCC at all. When answered greater than $0, the filer's farmer-or-rancher status becomes a genuine condition of allowance and must be answered too, or the deduction refuses Incomplete rather than silently assuming either ceiling. No carryover is modeled: a QCC that exceeds this year's ceiling carries forward for FIFTEEN years (not the five this module's other carryover lots track), a disclosed gap rather than a mis-modeled one. Dollar, non-negative.
THIS IS THE FILER'S OWN GIFT. It EXCLUDES a partnership's, S corporation's or Form 8865 partnership's Schedule K-1 box 13/12 code G qualified conservation contribution passed through to the filer, which /k1CharitableQCC totals from the recorded K-1 documents and /charitableQCCIncludingK1 adds to this entry before the ceiling test. Entering that amount here as well would state the same gift twice; the graph cannot tell a double entry from a genuinely larger direct gift, which is why the carve is stated on the intake rather than enforced in arithmetic. The farmer/rancher ceiling test now runs against the COMBINED figure, not this writable alone, so a K-1 code G pass-through also makes /writableCharitableQualifiedFarmerOrRancher a genuine condition of allowance, even when this writable itself is never answered.

Fact.Name: Qualified farmer or rancher status for the QCC 100%-of-AGI limit
Fact.Description:
IRC 170(b)(1)(E)(iv)-(v): whether the filer is a "qualified farmer or rancher" for the year -- gross income from the trade or business of farming more than 50% of the filer's total gross income for the year -- AND the donated property carries a restriction that it remain available for agriculture or livestock production. When both are true, the qualified conservation contribution ceiling (/writableCharitableQualifiedConservationContribution) is 100% of AGI instead of 50%. Asked only when /charitableQCCIncludingK1 -- the filer's own QCC plus any Schedule K-1 code G pass-through -- is greater than $0; a return with neither never sees this question. A return with a QCC amount (direct or K-1) but no answer here refuses the QCC deduction Incomplete rather than defaulting to either ceiling.
ONE ANSWER GOVERNS BOTH SOURCES, per IRC 170(b)(1)(E)(iv)-(v)'s own terms: farmer-or-rancher status is a taxpayer-YEAR status, not a per-gift one, and both partner instructions ask the 100%-versus-50% question of the PARTNER, not of the entity, for a K-1 code G contribution. DISCLOSED EDGE: the K-1 code G population is by definition property already restricted to agricultural or livestock use, so only the status half of this compound question is a genuine condition for that leg; the property-restriction half remains a genuine condition for the DIRECT gift alone. A filer who meets the income test but whose OWN direct gift is not agriculture-restricted, and who ALSO receives a K-1 code G pass-through, cannot answer differently for the two legs with one Boolean -- answering FALSE for the direct gift's own restriction understates the K-1 leg's ceiling. Not split, because the population is vanishingly narrow (both a direct QCC and a K-1 code G pass-through in the same year) and a second writable would ask most filers a question that never matters; named here and in the module's own records for whoever narrows it. Boolean.

Fact.Name: Deductible qualified conservation contribution after its own AGI ceiling
Fact.Description:
The smaller of (a) /charitableQCCIncludingK1 -- the filer's own QCC entry PLUS any Schedule K-1 code G pass-through, floored at zero on both legs -- and (b) the QCC's own ceiling: 50% of AGI (100% for a qualifying farmer or rancher) minus the filer's deduction for every OTHER current-year charitable contribution -- the eight Deductible facts this module already computes for the 60/50/30/20-percent tiers and the three current-year carryover-in chains (/charitableCashDeductible, /charitableCapitalGainDeductible, /charitable30PctOrgCashDeductible, /charitable30PctOrgNonCashDeductible, /charitable30PctOrgCapitalGainDeductible, /charitableCarryoverInDeductible, /charitableCashCarryoverInDeductible, /charitableCapGainCarryoverInDeductible) -- NOT /charitableContributionsDeduction itself, which would close a cycle now that this fact is one of its addends. IRC 170(b)(1)(E)(iii) coordinates a QCC OUTSIDE subparagraphs (A)-(D), which is why it reads the eight underlying Deductible facts directly rather than their already-coordinated total.
NOT CLAIMING is complete-safe $0: a return whose combined figure is zero or less -- no direct entry, no K-1 code G pass-through, or a negative direct entry that the combining fact has already floored -- deducts $0 here and never asks the farmer/rancher question, so no pre-existing scenario moves (the combined figure IS the direct writable on every return with no K-1 code G pass-through).
CLAIMING (the combined figure greater than $0) makes farmer/rancher status a genuine condition of allowance for BOTH sources at once: answered TRUE selects the 100%-of-AGI ceiling, answered FALSE selects 50%, and UNANSWERED refuses this fact Incomplete -- the ceiling is never guessed, whether the claim arrived directly or only through a K-1. Both answered branches are guarded with the IsComplete-first idiom (All(IsComplete(farmer), farmer) / All(IsComplete(farmer), Not(farmer))) so a genuinely Incomplete farmer/rancher fact cannot collapse either branch to a false match; with no third branch to catch it, an Incomplete farmer/rancher answer leaves every Case unmatched and the fact itself Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Qualified conservation contribution carryover to 2026
Fact.Description: The current-year combined QCC amount (/charitableQCCIncludingK1: the filer's own entry plus any Schedule K-1 code G pass-through) that exceeds its allowed Schedule A line-12 deduction, preserved as a carry-out for the next tax year. Qualified conservation contributions carry forward for fifteen years under IRC 170(b)(1)(E)(ii), unlike the ordinary five-year charitable carryover pool. This is a records-side export only: the 2025 return does not apply it again, and the ordinary /charitableCarryover intentionally excludes QCC. A return with no direct QCC and no K-1 code G pass-through is complete-safe $0; a combined amount whose farmer/rancher ceiling is still unanswered remains Incomplete, because it reads /charitableQualifiedConservationContributionDeductible, rather than silently losing the carry-out.

Fact.Name: Schedule A line 14 — total charitable deduction after AGI limits
Fact.Description: Schedule A line 14 = deductible cash to 50%-orgs (line 11 after 60%) + deductible capital-gain property to 50%-orgs (line 12 after 30% / the 50% ceiling) + deductible cash to 30%-orgs (30%-tier) + deductible capital-gain property to 30%-orgs (20%-tier) + deductible prior-year carryover (line 13 after the remaining 50% ceiling headroom) + the deductible qualified conservation contribution (its own 50%/100%-of-AGI ceiling, coordinated outside the other tiers per IRC 170(b)(1)(E)(iii)). Replaces the raw line-11 + line-12 sum in total itemized deductions. Every addend besides the two 50%-org base terms is complete-safe 0 when its writable is absent, so this is value-identical for every scenario that never answers one of them. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).

Fact.Name: Charitable contribution carryover to 2026 (REPORTED, not applied)
Fact.Description:
US8-4: the gifts disallowed by the AGI limits this year = (cash − deductible cash) + (property − deductible property) + (30%-org cash − its deductible) + (30%-org capital-gain property − its deductible) (the two 30%-org excess terms are complete-safe inline switches — 0 when those writables are absent, so this stays byte-identical on every scenario without them). REPORTED as an output only — the single-year demo never applies it to a future year (the carryforward posture; carryovers keep their 5-year window and character in reality). Complete-safe with the deductible chain.
FIFTH ADDEND: /charitable30PctOrgNonCashCarryoverToNextYear, the current-year excess of the 30%-organization NONCASH pool (K-1 box 13 code D and the "for the use of" noncash gifts) over its own allowed deduction. That tier had a deductible fact and no excess term, so its disallowed part was dropped from the reported carryover while its cash sibling's was counted. Complete-safe 0 when the tier's writables are absent, so every committed scenario is byte-identical -- measured, 0 moves on this fact across the 142 committed scheduleA + taxCalculations fixtures. Still REPORTED, not applied.

Fact.Name: Unabsorbed prior-year charitable carryover surviving to 2026 (recomputed)
Fact.Description:
Recomputed carryover-OUT: of the prior-year carryover the filer brought IN, how much this year's AGI ceilings did NOT absorb. Pub 526 states the survival rule for the part that does not fit — a contribution over the limit "isn't deductible for the year. It can be carried over to later years" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p526.pdf, page 26).
NOT THE SAME NUMBER AS /charitableCarryover, and the two are deliberately kept as separate exported facts rather than summed. /charitableCarryover is THIS year's own excess — the four current-year gift tiers minus what each tier's ceiling allowed — and carries no carry-IN term at all (verified by reading its body: its addends are /writableCharitableCash, /writableCharitableNonCash and the two 30%-org writables, each less its own deductible). This fact is the OTHER half: the unabsorbed remainder of the carryover the filer brought in. They are disjoint quantities with different 5-year vintages — this year's disallowed gifts start a fresh window, an unabsorbed carry-IN continues an older one — so adding them would produce a single undated number that is wrong for both.
THEY ARE DISJOINT BUT NOT INDEPENDENT. The claim above that /charitableCarryover "carries no carry-IN term at all" is true of its ARITHMETIC and was misleading about its VALUE: since the 30%-limit tiers began subtracting /attestedCharitableCarryoverIn50PctOrgs from their overall-ceiling headroom, a larger carryover-IN holds those tiers down and so makes /charitableCarryover LARGER. The two numbers therefore trade against each other under one 50%-of-AGI ceiling, and Pub 526 Carryovers Example 2 is the demonstration: the same $2,000 sits in /charitableCarryover (a fresh window) after the correction where it used to sit in this fact (an old, partly spent one). Which of the two holds a dollar is precisely the question records contract /charitableCarryoverLotVintage exists for, and it is now decided correctly at the boundary this module can see, while the VINTAGE of the dollars remains unrepresentable.
THE MUTUAL EXCLUSION IS THE WHOLE DESIGN, and getting it wrong is the trap this fact exists to avoid. Schedule A line 13's carry-IN is modeled THREE ways, and they are made mutually exclusive in the graph rather than by convention: /charitableCarryoverInDeductible is the BLENDED fallback (50%-of-AGI ceiling) and is SUPPRESSED TO $0 whenever either character-split writable is answered, with /charitableCashCarryoverInDeductible (60% cash ceiling) and /charitableCapGainCarryoverInDeductible (30% capital-gain ceiling under a 50% overall cap) taking over. A carry-OUT computed as the single subtraction (/writableCharitableCarryoverFromPriorTaxYear minus /charitableCarryoverInDeductible) would therefore report the ENTIRE blended carryover as unabsorbed for any filer on the split path — the blended deductible is $0 there by design, not because nothing was absorbed — and would then add the split residues on top. This fact mirrors the shipping suppression instead: each residue pairs a writable with ITS OWN deductible, and the blended leg goes to $0 on exactly the condition the shipping deductible uses.
EACH LEG IS COMPLETE-SAFE IN ITS OWN RIGHT, which is why all three are inline Switches rather than a single guarded Add: on the split path a filer may answer the cash carryover and not the capital-gain one, so an unguarded read of the missing writable would send this whole fact Incomplete by contagion. The idiom is the one /charitableCarryover already uses for its two 30%-org terms in this same module.
NON-NEGATIVE BY CONSTRUCTION, with the floor kept anyway. Every deductible above is a LesserOf whose first term is the writable itself, so a residue can never be negative; the GreaterOf against $0 on each leg is defensive and documents the intent rather than correcting anything.
WHAT THIS FACT DOES NOT DO, stated plainly because the honest conversion of that ledger row is SPLIT and this is the buildable half. It emits an UNDATED carryover. A charitable carryover expires 5 years after the contribution year and next year's deduction consumes carryovers oldest-first, and neither the contribution year of the carry-IN nor its remaining window is representable — /writableCharitableCarryoverFromPriorTaxYear and its two typed siblings are undated dollar amounts. The Schedule A line 13 instruction's own 2021/60%-limit sentence is the proof that vintage matters (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sca.pdf, page 11). So EXPIRY IS THE FILER'S TO TRACK: this number is what survived the ceilings, not what survived the calendar. Dated, expiring, ordered carryover lots would be new attested state rather than a computation, and they are records contract /charitableCarryoverLotVintage.
CHARACTER IS PRESERVED WHERE THE GRAPH HAS IT, and lost where it does not: on the split path the two residues keep their 60% and 30% origins in the legs that produced them, but this fact reports their SUM, because Schedule A line 13 is one printed line and next year's re-entry surface is the same three writables. A filer on the split path who needs to re-enter by character has both legs available in this fact's own arithmetic; a filer on the blended path never had the character to begin with.
CONSUMER: none in this return, exactly like /charitableCarryover above — the reader is next year's Schedule A line 13. Exported, not wired, and not mef: no line of the 2025 return transmits it. WORLD-1 SAFETY: additive and value-NEUTRAL — nothing consumes it, so no line of this return moves and no committed scenario changes.

Fact.Name: Of the Schedule A line 5d amount, the part that is real estate taxes (line 5b)
Fact.Description:
The state and local real estate taxes on Schedule A line 5b; foreign taxes paid on real estate are left out, because section 164(b)(6)(A) bars foreign real property taxes for 2018 through 2025 and the line 5b instructions list them among the amounts not to include. The real estate tax PORTION of /writableStateLocalTaxes, collected only so the Publication 570 chapter 4 apportionment can reach it. Optional, and $0 when unanswered.
[THE NEXT PARAGRAPH IS SUPERSEDED AND IS LEFT STANDING AS HISTORY. Lines 5a and 5c now have their own intakes and /scheduleALine5dStateAndLocalTaxes adds all three printed components when the filer answers either of them, so the split IS modelled. THIS FACT'S ROLE WIDENED RATHER THAN CHANGED: on a return that answers only the combined total it is still purely the apportionment portion, and on a return that splits 5a or 5c out it is ALSO the line 5b addend of the derived total, which is what the printed line says it is. It is deliberately NOT part of the mutual exclusion test /scheduleALine5dComponentLinesAnswered - see that fact for why answering 5b alone must keep reading the combined intake.]
WHY A PORTION INTAKE RATHER THAN A 5a/5b/5c SPLIT. /writableStateLocalTaxes is Schedule A line 5d, which COMBINES state and local income-or-sales taxes, real estate taxes and personal property taxes; this module has never modelled the split. Pub. 570 names REAL ESTATE TAXES specifically in the class of deductions that "do not specifically apply to any particular type of income" and apportions them at 96,000/120,000 x 10,000 = 8,000, "enter on line 5b of Schedule A" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 34). It says nothing about state INCOME taxes, and the omission is not obviously an oversight: a tax levied on particular income has a real argument for being "specifically applicable" to it, which would make it fully DISALLOWED rather than apportioned. Splitting line 5d properly is its own unit; asking for the one component the publication names is the smallest honest step, and it leaves the harder question visibly open instead of resolving it by silence.
THE $0 TAIL IS TAXPAYER-FAVOURABLE AND IS STATED RATHER THAN BURIED: a filer with real estate taxes who is never asked this has them apportioned by nothing, so the SALT deduction stays too large. That is the same posture every optional intake in this unit takes, and the population is refused today by ctcOdc /knockoutPossessionOrPuertoRicoIncomeExclusion.
NOT CROSS-CHECKED AGAINST LINE 5d, because the engine has no cross-fact Limit: an answer larger than /writableStateLocalTaxes would make /allowableStateLocalTaxes smaller than the apportionment alone warrants. Min 0 is enforced; the upper bound is the filer's.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Dollar, integer cents, NON-NEGATIVE. interpretation:provisional.
LEAVE OUT the real estate taxes of a property listed as a Schedule E rental: the personal part of those taxes is added by the return (scheduleE:/rentalPropertiesPersonalRealEstateTaxes), and the rental part is on Schedule E.
LEAVE OUT the real estate taxes you entered on Form 8829 for a home you use for a business (scheduleC:/scheduleCs/*/writableForm8829IndirectRealEstateTaxes): the return adds their personal part (scheduleC:/form8829PersonalHomeRealEstateTaxesTotal) and puts the business part on Form 8829.

Fact.Name: Real estate taxes within line 5d, complete-safe
Fact.Description:
= /writableRealEstateTaxesIncludedInStateLocalTaxes when answered, else $0. The IsComplete/Switch guard idiom. The $0 tail makes /allowableStateLocalTaxes equal to /writableStateLocalTaxes exactly, so an unanswered return is byte-identical. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).
PLUS scheduleE:/rentalPropertiesPersonalRealEstateTaxes, the personal part of the real estate taxes of rental properties the filer also used personally (Schedule E line 16 whole-property taxes less their rental part). Pub. 527 tells the filer to report that personal portion on line 5b; the return figures it, so the filer's own line 5b entry leaves those taxes out. PLUS scheduleC:/form8829PersonalHomeRealEstateTaxesTotal, the personal part of the real estate taxes of a home used for a business that files Form 8829 (the home's taxes less Line 11 Worksheet line 6), on a return that itemizes.

Fact.Name: Schedule A line 5d carries an amount and its real-estate part was never asked
Fact.Description:
TRUE when this return enters a non-zero Schedule A line 5d AND does not say how much of it is real estate taxes. A KNOCKOUT INPUT and nothing else: it feeds ctcOdc /knockoutPossessionOrPuertoRicoIncomeExclusion. It changes no deduction.
THE COMPANION-INTAKE FAILURE, and it is the same shape as schedule1A:/possessionUntreatedTipsOrOvertime rather than a Schedule A peculiarity. Publication 570 chapter 4 names REAL ESTATE TAXES in the apportioned class and prints the worked figure — "Real estate taxes ... 96,000 / 120,000 x 10,000 = 8,000 (enter on line 5b of Schedule A)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 34). This module apportions them at /allowableStateLocalTaxes. But line 5d is a COMBINED intake — state and local income-or-sales, real estate and personal property taxes in one figure — so the apportionment needs the filer to name the real-estate part, and /writableRealEstateTaxesIncludedInStateLocalTaxes is optional with a $0 tail. A filer with real estate taxes inside line 5d who is never ASKED which part they are has them apportioned by NOTHING: the whole of 5d survives as the non-real-estate remainder and the built treatment goes inert. Direction: SALT deduction too LARGE, taxpayer-FAVOURABLE. THAT INTAKE ALREADY SAID SO AND NAMED THIS FACT'S CONSUMER AS THE PROTECTION: "THE $0 TAIL IS TAXPAYER-FAVOURABLE AND IS STATED RATHER THAN BURIED ... the population is refused today by ctcOdc /knockoutPossessionOrPuertoRicoIncomeExclusion." The narrowing of that knockout would have withdrawn the protection while leaving the sentence standing; this fact is what keeps the sentence true.
NOT THE SAME THING AS THE 5d REMAINDER ITSELF, and the distinction is the whole reason this fact is narrow. Once the real-estate part IS named, the rest of line 5d is left unapportioned DELIBERATELY and CORRECTLY: 26 CFR 1.861-8(e)(6) makes the section 164 deduction "definitely related and allocable to the gross income with respect to which such state income taxes are imposed" (26 CFR 1.861-8, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-1.861-8, the RIGHT column of a two-column extraction), and a definitely-related deduction follows its income rather than a gross-income ratio. So a non-zero remainder is NOT a refusal condition — only the unasked question is.
AN ANSWERED $0 DISCHARGES IT, deliberately: a filer who says none of line 5d is real estate has ANSWERED, and the apportionment is then correct at zero rather than merely absent. A DATA-COMPLETENESS test, the same class as formW2s /hasW2ValidationErrors, so the filer has a route through the knockout rather than a wall.
COMPLETE ON EVERY RETURN BY CONSTRUCTION, which is load-bearing rather than tidy: it feeds a knockout, and an Incomplete member would leave flow:/flowIsKnockedOut unresolved on returns that resolve it today. The IsComplete guard leads the All and IsComplete never propagates incompleteness, the same shape /pdfStandardDeductionModifiedForPossessionExclusion uses. It resolves FALSE on every return that never answers line 5d — which is every committed scenario that does not itemize, and every committed itemizer answers 5d without a possession exclusion, so the outer conjunct at the knockout is false there regardless.

Fact.Name: A prior-year charitable carryover comes in, and nothing apportions it
Fact.Description:
TRUE when this return brings a prior-year charitable contribution carryover in on ANY of the three Schedule A line 13 intake paths. A KNOCKOUT INPUT and nothing else: it feeds ctcOdc /knockoutPossessionOrPuertoRicoIncomeExclusion, which refuses a possession return only where the Publication 570 chapter 4 treatment cannot be applied to the whole of it. It changes no deduction.
THE GAP IT DETECTS, MEASURED ON THIS MODULE RATHER THAN INHERITED. The Publication 570 apportionment covers the CURRENT-year charitable gifts — /allowableCharitableCash, /allowableCharitableNonCash, /allowableCharitable30PctOrgCash and /allowableCharitable30PctOrgCapitalGain each multiply by the Publication 570 fraction. NO carryover fact does. Measured by walking every Dependency of /charitableCarryoverInDeductible, /charitableCashCarryoverInDeductible, /charitableCapGainCarryoverInDeductible, the ten /charitableCashCarryoverAllowed* and /charitableCapGainCarryoverAllowed* vintage steps and /attestedCharitableCarryoverIn50PctOrgs: not one of them reads income:/grossIncomeSubjectToUsTax, directly or transitively through an apportioned sibling. The carryover reaches line 13 as the raw attested amount, capped only by the AGI ceilings. Direction: carryover deducted in full, deduction too LARGE, taxpayer-FAVOURABLE.
⚠ AND THE APPORTIONMENT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS A GAP RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT CALL. The earlier position was "Publication 570 says nothing about a carryover and there are two defensible readings, so do not guess". That is no longer the position: 26 CFR 1.933-1(c) routes the disallowance to 26 CFR 1.861-8, and section 1.861-8(e)(12)(i) is on point — "The deduction for charitable contributions that is allowed under sections 170, 873(b)(2), and 882(c)(1)(B) is definitely related and allocable to all of the taxpayer's gross income. The deduction allocated under this paragraph (e)(12)(i) shall be apportioned ... on the basis of the relative amounts of gross income" (26 CFR 1.861-8, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-1.861-8, the LEFT column of a two-column extraction). Section 170 is the carryover's own section, so the carryover takes the same apportionment as the gift. The rule is KNOWN and UNBUILT, which is exactly what a knockout input is for. ⚠⚠ A CLAIM IN dictionary/ty2025/SOURCES.md IS CORRECTED BY THIS FACT. Its possession-apportionment section says of charitable carryovers: "apportioning them is right — WHICH IS WHAT SHIPS." The first half is right and is quoted above. The second half is FALSE, on the walk recorded two paragraphs up: no carryover fact carries the fraction. The regulation was read and its conclusion was recorded as though building it had followed; it had not. Left standing, that sentence would have retired this condition by assertion.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT A TERM HERE — THE SCHEDULE A LINE 5d REMAINDER. An earlier draft of this fact refused on it, because /allowableStateLocalTaxes apportions only the real-estate portion and leaves the rest of line 5d untouched, and that was recorded as an open taxpayer-favourable tail. IT IS NOT ONE. Section 1.861-8(e)(6) settles it the other way: "The deduction for state and local taxes (state income taxes) allowed by section 164 is considered definitely related and allocable to the gross income with respect to which such state income taxes are imposed" (26 CFR 1.861-8, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-1.861-8, the RIGHT column). A definitely related deduction follows its income; it is not apportioned on a gross-income ratio. So leaving the remainder alone is the CORRECT treatment, not an unbuilt one, and refusing on it would refuse a return this dictionary computes right. WHAT LINE 5d DOES CONTRIBUTE IS A DIFFERENT FACT, /possessionRealEstatePortionUnanswered above: not the surviving remainder, but the UNASKED question that leaves the real-estate apportionment inert. Distinguishing the two is the whole point of splitting them.
WHY IT TESTS ANSWERED-NESS RATHER THAN A NON-ZERO AMOUNT, stated because it OVER-refuses and that is a real cost. The thirteen carryover-in intakes reach line 13 through three mutually exclusive paths whose blending and vintage-suppression rules are themselves conditional (/charitableCarryoverVintageSlotsAnswered), so no single acyclic "how much came in" figure exists — the one dollar aggregate that is acyclic, /attestedCharitableCarryoverIn50PctOrgs, exists to be a SUBTRAHEND in the 30%-org tiers and is not the whole line-13 amount. A filer who answers a carryover of exactly $0 is therefore refused when nothing would have moved. That errs toward refusal, which is the direction a knockout input should err in.
COMPLETE ON EVERY RETURN BY CONSTRUCTION, which is load-bearing rather than tidy: it feeds a knockout, and an Incomplete member would leave flow:/flowIsKnockedOut unresolved on returns that resolve it today. Every term is an IsComplete or a fact built only from IsCompletes, and IsComplete never propagates incompleteness, so this resolves FALSE on every return that answers no carryover — which is every committed scenario.

Fact.Name: State and local taxes allowable on Schedule A line 5d after the Pub. 570 apportionment
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 5d as ENTERED: the non-real-estate remainder of /scheduleALine5dStateAndLocalTaxes, PLUS the real estate portion apportioned by the Publication 570 chapter 4 fraction. With no exclusion, or no real estate portion answered, this IS /scheduleALine5dStateAndLocalTaxes.
THE LINE 5d TERM IS NOT THE RAW COMBINED INTAKE: it is /scheduleALine5dStateAndLocalTaxes, which adds the printed components 5a, 5b and 5c when the filer split them out and falls through to /writableStateLocalTaxes otherwise. Nothing else about this fact changed, and a return that never answers line 5a or 5c reads the same number it read before.
ONLY THE REAL ESTATE PORTION MOVES, and that is the point of the split rather than a limitation of it: Pub. 570 names real estate taxes in the apportioned class and is silent on state INCOME taxes, which have a real argument for being specifically applicable to the income they are levied on - and specifically-applicable deductions are DISALLOWED OUTRIGHT (lines 2255-2257), not apportioned. Apportioning the whole of line 5d would apply the wrong one of the publication's two rules to the income-tax component.
APPORTIONED BEFORE THE SALT CAP, consistent with every other Schedule A class in this unit: this fact feeds /saltDeduction's LesserOf against /saltDeductionLimit, so the cap runs on the apportioned figure exactly as the publication's "enter on Schedule A only the allowable portion" instruction requires.
THE REMAINDER IS NOT APPORTIONED AND THAT IS A DISCLOSED GAP, not a finding of correctness: this fill does not decide whether state income taxes are apportioned, fully disallowed, or untouched. It preserves today's treatment for them and moves only what the publication names. Direction if they should have been apportioned: SALT too large, taxpayer-favourable. Fact.Name: Estate tax on income in respect of a decedent from Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) box 10 (Schedule A line 16)
Fact.Description:
The rounded total of box 10, "Estate tax deduction", over every Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) the filer recorded in scheduleE:/form1041K1s. This is the line 16 closed list item "Federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent": the beneficiary of an estate or trust that distributed income in respect of a decedent may deduct the portion of the estate tax imposed on the decedent's estate that is attributable to that IRD, and the printed K-1 sends the figure to Schedule A line 16 in one hop.
COMPLETE SAFE IN BOTH HALVES. The whole CollectionSum sits inside an IsComplete Switch on the scheduleE:/form1041K1s collection itself, defaulting to $0, so a return that never opened the estate and trust K-1 section resolves Complete $0 instead of Placeholder and Schedule A line 16 keeps the completeness it has today; and each item contributes through ../estateTaxDeductionOnIrdOrZero, so a K-1 recorded for its income boxes alone contributes a Complete $0. NOT AN AGI LIMITED CONTRIBUTION AND NOT A MISCELLANEOUS ITEMIZED DEDUCTION: the IRD estate tax deduction survives the section 67(g) suspension because it is named on the line 16 closed list in its own right, which is why it enters the total beside the other closed list items rather than through the 2 percent floor machinery this dictionary does not model.

Fact.Name: Schedule A line 16 — other itemized deductions
Fact.Description:
Schedule A line 16 total = deductible gambling losses (capped at winnings) + the general other-itemized write-in + casualty and theft losses of income-producing property + the IRC 1341 claim-of-right repayment over $3,000. Gated on /claimsItemizedDeductions (0 when not itemizing). All three terms are complete-safe, so this is always complete and resolves 0 for every scenario without it — it adds 0 to /totalItemizedDeductions and keeps the itemized-vs-standard greater-of value-identical unless line 16 is actually used. THE THIRD TERM is form4684:/incomeProducingCasualtyLoss, Form 4684 Section B lines 32 and 38b — column (b)(ii), income-producing property. The line-16 instructions are a CLOSED list ("Only the expenses listed next can be deducted on line 16") and it names this item explicitly: "Casualty and theft losses of income-producing property (including losses from financial scams) from Form 4684, lines 32 and 38b, or Form 4797, line 18a" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sca.pdf, page 11). Note the "or": Form 4797 line 18a is an ALTERNATIVE route to this same line, taken up by THE FIFTH TERM below; the argument, re-derived from the printed forms, is in form4684:/incomeProducingCasualtyLoss's Description. Positive, like its two siblings. Complete 0 on every return that does not attest income-producing property, so this addend is byte-identical additive for the whole existing corpus. NOT ON THIS LINE, to keep the two casualty destinations apart: the Section A personal-use casualty deduction is Form 4684 line 18 and belongs on line 15 (form4684:/casualtyLossDeduction, /totalItemizedDeductions' own addend), and column (b)(i) business-property losses leave on Form 4797 line 14 to Schedule 1 line 4, never reaching Schedule A at all. THE FIFTH TERM is form4797:/lossFromForm4684ColumnBiiOnLineEleven, Form 4797 line 18a - the SECOND of the two routes the closed list names. It is computed. THE "or" IS EXCLUSIVE AND THE ENGINE ENFORCES IT rather than relying on this note: 18a is gated on a positive Form 4797 line 3, which exists only on the Form 4684 LINE-39 branch (line 37 at or below line 36), while form4684:/incomeProducingCasualtyLoss's long-term half, line 38b, exists only on the LINE-38 branch (line 37 above line 36). The two branches are complementary, so at most one of the two addends can carry the long-term column (b)(ii) loss. THE SHORT-TERM HALF OF /incomeProducingCasualtyLoss (Form 4684 line 32) is NOT in that exclusion and does not need to be: it is a different loss, on property held one year or less, which line 18a's own operand (Form 4684 line 35, column (b)(ii)) does not contain. COMPLETE-SAFETY: the new addend's first Switch arm returns a literal Dollar 0 without reading anything on every return that has no Form 4684 line-39 gain, so it is byte-identical additive for the whole existing corpus AND it does not import the Result.Incomplete that form4797:/netSection1231GainOrLoss carries on a refused disposition - the reason that gate is ordered first is written on the fact itself.
THE SEVENTH TERM is form4684:/netQualifiedDisasterLoss — the SAME fact standardDeduction:/fullStandardDeduction already adds on the standard-deduction route. i4684's own Line 15 "Net loss" instruction states BOTH arms in one paragraph: "If you are itemizing your deductions, enter the amount on line 16 of Schedule A (Form 1040) ... and 'Net Qualified Disaster Loss.' If you are claiming the increased standard deduction, enter the amount on line 16 of Schedule A (Form 1040) ... and 'Net Qualified Disaster Loss.'" (i4684:554-573). Before this fill, only the standard-deduction arm was built — an itemizer with a qualified disaster loss lost the whole benefit (min(QDL, itemized − standard) understated, taxpayer-adverse). THE TWO ROUTES NEVER BOTH FIRE: this addend sits inside the SAME /claimsItemizedDeductions-gated Switch arm every other line-16 addend does, so it is $0 on the standard-deduction route by construction — that route's QDL increase stays exactly where standardDeduction.xml already puts it. An itemizer's Schedule A line 17 total (and therefore taxCalculations:/wantsStandardDeduction's comparison) now correctly includes the loss; Form 1040 line 12 receives it through the ordinary itemized-deductions chain rather than losing it. COMPLETE-SAFE $0 on every return with no qualified disaster attestation (form4684:/netQualifiedDisasterLoss's own gate), so this addend is byte-identical additive for the whole existing corpus. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Schedule CA (540), Schedule CA (540NR)).

Not rounded and not gated on itemizing: /otherItemizedDeductions (the printed line 16) and the two legs of the section 1341 comparison, /otherItemizedDeductionsWithClaimOfRightRepayment and /otherItemizedDeductionsWithoutClaimOfRightRepayment, each apply the itemizing gate and the one Round, so the printed line and both legs add exactly the same items. Every addend is complete safe $0 where it does not apply.

Fact.Description: Deprecated. Retained so that saved returns holding this key still load. Not asked, and not read by any computation: the section 1341 method is not a filer choice. IRC 1341(a) makes the year's tax the lesser of the tax computed with the deduction and the tax computed without it minus the earlier-year decrease, so /electsClaimOfRightRepaymentDeduction reads the computed comparison taxCalculations:/claimOfRightDeductionGivesLesserTax.
